The graphs and the files

Source: vignettes/graphs.Rmd
graphs.Rmd

This vignette goes through everything a run of vp_generate() finds, one result at a time, on the Mi Band 3 of Get started: the features that are in every band or in none, the three graphs of strong relationships, the atomic sets, the minimal form, the kernel and the two reports of the run. Then it checks and explains the results, compares versions of a model, and ends with the options of vp_generate(), formulas made by other tools, and what happens when a model is wrong. Each result is also a file, and the vignette shows the files too, because other programs can read them.

library(variplex)
library(dplyr)
band <- vp_generate(
  vp_example("miband3_realized.uvl"),
  output_dir = "out",
  or_graph = TRUE,
  kernel = TRUE,
  keep_dimacs = TRUE
)
show_file <- function(ending) {
  writeLines(readLines(paste0("out/miband3_realized__", ending)))
}

show_file() prints a file of the run; it is only a shortcut for this vignette.

Core, dead and variable features

Before looking at pairs of features, vp_generate() sets aside the 5 abstract features, which are not parts of a band, and looks at each other feature alone. It sorts it into one of three kinds, one of the classic analyses of feature models Benavides et al. (2010); Trinidad et al. (2008). Only the third kind is a real choice, and only the third kind gets a question to the solver:

Kind of feature Mi Band 3 Is a question to the solver worth asking?
core: in every valid configuration 8 No. Supposing that it is selected changes nothing, because it always is. Every other feature “requires” it, which tells nothing about the choices you can make.
dead: in no valid configuration 0 No. It can never be selected, so “suppose it is selected” has no answer. A dead feature is almost always a mistake in the model (When something is wrong).
variable: in some valid configurations and not in others 11 Yes, one question each: “suppose this feature is selected: which features must then be selected too, and which can then not be selected at all?”

One quick check of all the features at once tells the three kinds apart before the expensive questions start. That is why the first run of Get started said Querying 11 variables: 24 features, of which 5 are abstract, 8 are core and 0 are dead, leave 11 questions, and these 11 features are exactly the dots of the graphs. Two words of that message need a gloss: variables are the variables of the logic formula (in a formula translated from UVL each variable is one feature), and (input filter) says that the variables not worth a question were set aside before asking, which is the normal way to work.

The model again, with the core features in green and the abstract features, which variplex leaves out, in yellow. The 11 white features are the ones that can vary; they are the dots of the graphs.

vp_features() gives every feature with its status; the core features are also in the file __core.txt:

vp_features(band) |> count(status)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>   status       n
#>   <chr>    <int>
#> 1 core         8
#> 2 variable    11
show_file("core.txt")
#> 0 "FitnessMonitor"
#> 0 "SleepTracker"
#> 0 "VibrateAlert"
#> 0 "Call"
#> 0 "Notification"
#> 0 "Pedometer"
#> 0 "Accelerometer"
#> 0 "Bluetooth"

They are no surprise: the concrete features that hang from the root through mandatory links only (the root and the headings on the way are abstract, so they are not listed). In the file, each line has a number and a name. The number is the position of the feature in the graphs, and it is 0 because core features are not drawn in the graphs: they are in every band, so every feature “requires” them, and drawing that would only add noise (Showing core features and abstract ones shows how to draw them anyway).

The file of dead features is empty, which is good news:

show_file("dead.txt")

More than half of this model is not a choice at all, and variplex asks only about the rest. In a formula made by another tool it also skips the helper variables of the translation, and there the saving is large: the formula of Linux 3.13 has 23,838 variables, and variplex asks only 7,100 questions (Formulas made by other tools).

The requires graph: “if I take this, I also get that”

In R, the requires graph is a tibble with one row per arrow: from requires to.

vp_links(band, "requires")
#> # A tibble: 21 x 2
#>    from               to            
#>    <chr>              <chr>         
#>  1 Screen             OLED          
#>  2 Screen             CapacityButton
#>  3 TouchScreen        Screen        
#>  4 TouchScreen        OLED          
#>  5 TouchScreen        CapacityButton
#>  6 OLED               Screen        
#>  7 OLED               CapacityButton
#>  8 CapacityButton     Screen        
#>  9 CapacityButton     OLED          
#> 10 ContactlessPayment NFC           
#> # i 11 more rows

The file __requires.net holds the same graph, as text:

show_file("requires.net")
#> *Vertices 11
#> 1 "Screen"
#> 2 "TouchScreen"
#> 3 "OLED"
#> 4 "CapacityButton"
#> 5 "ContactlessPayment"
#> 6 "MovementFilter"
#> 7 "HeartRateSensor"
#> 8 "BLEv40"
#> 9 "BLEv42"
#> 10 "BT40"
#> 11 "NFC"
#> *Arcs
#> 1 3
#> 1 4
#> 2 1
#> 2 3
#> 2 4
#> 3 1
#> 3 4
#> 4 1
#> 4 3
#> 5 11
#> 6 1
#> 6 3
#> 6 4
#> 6 8
#> 8 1
#> 8 3
#> 8 4
#> 9 1
#> 9 3
#> 9 4
#> 9 7

It has two parts.

  • After *Vertices 11 come the 11 features that can vary, numbered from 1.
  • After *Arcs come the relationships, one per line, as two numbers. The line 2 1 means: feature 2 requires feature 1, that is, TouchScreen requires Screen.

This format is called Pajek, and programs for network analysis read it directly (Using the results in other programs). The figure is the same graph as a drawing.

The requires graph of the Mi Band 3: 21 arrows among 11 features. An arrow from A to B says “every band with A has B”. The 3 features in the dashed box require each other.

Why so many arrows?

The model has only a handful of constraints, yet the graph has 21 arrows. The reason is that the graph is complete: it holds every “requires” that is true, not only those that somebody wrote. Three examples:

  • TouchScreen → Screen is written in the model: a child needs its parent.
  • MovementFilter → Screen is written nowhere. It follows from a chain: the movement filter needs BLE version 4.0 (constraint 1), which is a kind of BLE, and a band with BLE does not use classic Bluetooth, so it has a screen (constraint 4).
  • BLEv42 → HeartRateSensor is also written nowhere. A band with BLE version 4.2 has BLE, so it has a heart-rate sensor or a movement filter (constraint 2). But the movement filter needs version 4.0 (constraint 1), and a band has only one version. So it must be the heart-rate sensor.

You do not have to follow chains like these. That is the job of variplex. You read the answer: if the arrow is in the graph, the relationship holds in every valid band; if it is not, there is at least one valid band where it fails.

Try it

What do you get “for free” when you choose BLEv42?

vp_requirements(band, "BLEv42")
#> # A tibble: 4 x 1
#>   feature        
#>   <chr>          
#> 1 Screen         
#> 2 OLED           
#> 3 CapacityButton 
#> 4 HeartRateSensor

Screen, OLED, CapacityButton and HeartRateSensor (and BLE, an abstract feature, which the graphs leave out).

The excludes graph: “these two never go together” 

vp_links(band, "excludes")
#> # A tibble: 10 x 2
#>    from           to             
#>    <chr>          <chr>          
#>  1 Screen         BT40           
#>  2 TouchScreen    BT40           
#>  3 OLED           BT40           
#>  4 CapacityButton BT40           
#>  5 MovementFilter HeartRateSensor
#>  6 MovementFilter BLEv42         
#>  7 MovementFilter BT40           
#>  8 BLEv40         BLEv42         
#>  9 BLEv40         BT40           
#> 10 BLEv42         BT40

The row MovementFilter, HeartRateSensor means that the two are never in the same band. A conflict has no direction (if A excludes B, then B excludes A), so each pair is listed once. In the file __excludes.net the same features are followed by *Edges, each pair written with the smaller number first; a link without a direction is called an edge instead of an arc:

show_file("excludes.net")
#> *Vertices 11
#> 1 "Screen"
#> 2 "TouchScreen"
#> 3 "OLED"
#> 4 "CapacityButton"
#> 5 "ContactlessPayment"
#> 6 "MovementFilter"
#> 7 "HeartRateSensor"
#> 8 "BLEv40"
#> 9 "BLEv42"
#> 10 "BT40"
#> 11 "NFC"
#> *Edges
#> 1 10
#> 2 10
#> 3 10
#> 4 10
#> 6 7
#> 6 9
#> 6 10
#> 8 9
#> 8 10
#> 9 10
The excludes graph: 10 conflicts. A dashed red line joins two features that no band has together. BT40, the classic Bluetooth, is in conflict with almost everything.

Again, most of these conflicts are consequences. The model says that BT40 bands have no screen (constraint 5). variplex adds that they cannot have a touch screen, an OLED panel, a capacity button, a movement filter or any version of BLE either, because each of those needs a screen, directly or through a chain.

HeartRateSensor, NFC and ContactlessPayment are in few or no conflicts. Features like these are easy to add to a band. We come back to this idea with the kernel (The kernel: “can these go together?”).

The at-least-one graph: “one of the two, at least”

The first two graphs say what happens when you take a feature. A third graph says what happens when you leave one out. It costs a second question per feature, so it is made only when you ask for it, with or_graph = TRUE (as the run at the top of this vignette did). An edge between A and B means: no valid band lacks both.

vp_links(band, "atleastone")
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>   from           to   
#>   <chr>          <chr>
#> 1 Screen         BT40 
#> 2 OLED           BT40 
#> 3 CapacityButton BT40

There are 3 such edges, all with BT40: a band has classic Bluetooth, or it has a screen (and with it the other features of its atomic set, Atomic sets).

The at-least-one graph. A dotted green line joins two features of which every band has at least one.

Why BLEv40 and BLEv42 are not joined

In the model, BLEv40 and BLEv42 are the two alternatives of BLE, and an alternative group means “exactly one”. So why does no edge join them? Because the edge would say more than that: that every band has one of the two. And BLE is itself one of two alternatives. Bluetooth is mandatory and is either BLE or BT40, and two constraints, !Screen => BT40 and BT40 => !Screen, give BT40 to exactly the bands without a screen. Such a band has no BLE, and so neither BLEv40 nor BLEv42. Of the 24 valid bands, 18 have BLE, and each of them has exactly one of the two versions; the other 6 have neither, and all of them are bands without a screen, with BT40.

variplex can show it too. Add “neither version” to the model as a constraint, one line more at its end, and run it. The model is still valid (a model that no band satisfies would be an error), and in the bands that are left, BT40 is core while the screen and both versions are dead (and so is BLE, which is not listed, being abstract):

tail(readLines(vp_example("miband3_no_ble.uvl")), 1)
#> [1] "\t!BLEv40 & !BLEv42"
no_ble <- vp_generate(vp_example("miband3_no_ble.uvl"))
vp_features(no_ble) |> filter(status != "variable" | feature == "BT40")
#> # A tibble: 16 x 2
#>    feature        status
#>    <chr>          <chr> 
#>  1 FitnessMonitor core  
#>  2 SleepTracker   core  
#>  3 VibrateAlert   core  
#>  4 Call           core  
#>  5 Notification   core  
#>  6 Pedometer      core  
#>  7 Accelerometer  core  
#>  8 Bluetooth      core  
#>  9 BT40           core  
#> 10 Screen         dead  
#> 11 TouchScreen    dead  
#> 12 OLED           dead  
#> 13 CapacityButton dead  
#> 14 MovementFilter dead  
#> 15 BLEv40         dead  
#> 16 BLEv42         dead

So what the model says about the two versions is conditional: if a band has BLE, it has BLEv40 or BLEv42. That is a rule about three features, BLE → BLEv40 or BLEv42, and a graph joins two features at a time, so the rule has no edge of its own. The three graphs show what it means for pairs of the features they keep. BLE is abstract, so it is not one of them, but a band has BLE exactly when it has a screen (Atomic sets), and the screen speaks for it. Both versions require Screen, and they exclude each other. One level up, where the parent is mandatory, the alternative does become an edge: every band has Bluetooth, so every band has BLE or BT40, that is, a screen or BT40: the edge between Screen and BT40. What pairs cannot say is the subject of Limits and theory.

Everything about a pair

With the three graphs you know everything the model says about any two features. For two features A and B there are four cases: both, only A, only B, neither. Each graph rules out one case, and vp_pair() puts them together:

vp_pair(band, "TouchScreen", "Screen")
#> # A tibble: 4 x 5
#>   combination      a     b     possible ruled_out_by                 
#>   <chr>            <lgl> <lgl> <lgl>    <chr>                        
#> 1 both             TRUE  TRUE  TRUE     ""                           
#> 2 only TouchScreen TRUE  FALSE FALSE    "TouchScreen requires Screen"
#> 3 only Screen      FALSE TRUE  TRUE     ""                           
#> 4 neither          FALSE FALSE TRUE     ""
vp_pair(band, "Screen", "BT40")
#> # A tibble: 4 x 5
#>   combination a     b     possible ruled_out_by                      
#>   <chr>       <lgl> <lgl> <lgl>    <chr>                             
#> 1 both        TRUE  TRUE  FALSE    "Screen excludes BT40"            
#> 2 only Screen TRUE  FALSE TRUE     ""                                
#> 3 only BT40   FALSE TRUE  TRUE     ""                                
#> 4 neither     FALSE FALSE FALSE    "every product has Screen or BT40"
vp_pair(band, "BLEv40", "BLEv42")
#> # A tibble: 4 x 5
#>   combination a     b     possible ruled_out_by            
#>   <chr>       <lgl> <lgl> <lgl>    <chr>                   
#> 1 both        TRUE  TRUE  FALSE    "BLEv40 excludes BLEv42"
#> 2 only BLEv40 TRUE  FALSE TRUE     ""                      
#> 3 only BLEv42 FALSE TRUE  TRUE     ""                      
#> 4 neither     FALSE FALSE TRUE     ""
  • TouchScreen and Screen: “only A” never happens. That is TouchScreen requires Screen.
  • Screen and BT40: never both (a conflict) and never neither (an “at least one” edge). Every band has exactly one of them.
  • BLEv40 and BLEv42: never both (a conflict), but neither does happen, in the bands without BLE (Why BLEv40 and BLEv42 are not joined). So no at-least-one edge joins them.
  • NFC and HeartRateSensor (try it): everything happens. They are independent, and no graph joins them.
  • Screen and OLED: both or neither. They are in the same atomic set.

The at-least-one graph costs time: variplex asks two questions per feature instead of one (here 22 instead of 11). For big models the run takes about twice as long. That is why you have to ask for it.

Atomic sets: features that always travel together

Look again at the dashed box of the requires graph. Screen requires OLED, and OLED requires Screen. When two features require each other, a band has both or neither: for the purpose of choosing, they are one single decision. A group like this is an atomic set Benavides et al. (2010); Heß and Molt (2025):

vp_atomic_sets(band)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 3
#>     set feature        representative
#>   <int> <chr>          <chr>         
#> 1     1 Screen         Screen        
#> 2     1 OLED           Screen        
#> 3     1 CapacityButton Screen
show_file("atomic.txt")
#> Screen   OLED    CapacityButton

There is 1 atomic set, with 3 features. The file __atomic.txt lists the sets, one per line. The members are expected: OLED is a mandatory child of Screen, and CapacityButton a mandatory child of OLED. The set has one more member, which the graphs leave out because it is abstract, BLE, and that one is a discovery:

A band has a screen exactly when it uses Bluetooth Low Energy.

Nobody wrote that. It follows from constraints 4 and 5 (no screen means classic Bluetooth, and classic Bluetooth means no screen) together with the fact that every band has exactly one kind of Bluetooth. With abstract = "keep" (Showing core features and abstract ones), BLE is in the atomic set too.

The atomic set of the Mi Band 3. Its features require each other, so they are selected together or not at all. The first name of the set, Screen, is the representative of the set.

An atomic set is a group of features that behave as one. Find them and your model has fewer real decisions than it seems.

The minimal form: the graphs without repetitions

The complete graphs are exact, but they repeat themselves. MovementFilter points to BLEv40 and BLEv40 points to Screen; the arrow from MovementFilter to Screen adds nothing new. The figure shows in grey every arrow that follows from others.

The requires graph once more. The grey arrows follow from the blue ones; only the blue ones carry information.

vp_generate() writes the essential part of each graph in a file of its own, and vp_minimal() computes it from any model. Together with the atomic sets they are the minimal form:

__requires_skeleton.net, vp_skeleton() The skeleton: the arrows that do not follow from a chain of other arrows (the transitive reduction of the graph Aho et al. (1972)). Each atomic set appears once, under the name of its representative.
__excludes_primitive.net, vp_primitive_conflicts() The primitive conflicts: the conflicts that a feature has by itself, not because it requires something that has the conflict.
__atleastone_primitive.net, vp_primitive_atleastone() The “at least one” edges that do not follow from others (with or_graph = TRUE; here 1 of the 3). 
band_min <- vp_minimal(band)
band_min
#> variplex model "miband3_realized"
#>   features: 9 variable (the nodes of the graphs), 8 core, 0 dead
#>   requires: 6 arrows   excludes: 3 lines
#>   at least one: 1 lines
#>   minimal form: skeleton, primitive conflicts and primitive at-least-one lines;
#>   each atomic set is one node (1 sets)
vp_links(band_min, "requires")
#> # A tibble: 6 x 2
#>   from               to             
#>   <chr>              <chr>          
#> 1 TouchScreen        Screen         
#> 2 ContactlessPayment NFC            
#> 3 MovementFilter     BLEv40         
#> 4 BLEv40             Screen         
#> 5 BLEv42             Screen         
#> 6 BLEv42             HeartRateSensor
vp_links(band_min, "excludes")
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>   from           to             
#>   <chr>          <chr>          
#> 1 Screen         BT40           
#> 2 MovementFilter HeartRateSensor
#> 3 BLEv40         BLEv42

From 21 arrows to 6, and from 10 conflicts to 3. The figure draws them together (vp_plot(band_min) makes the same drawing), and it is the clearest picture of the model: 3 conflicts and 6 dependencies explain everything.

The minimal form of the requires and excludes graphs: every arrow and every red line of the complete graphs follows from this drawing.

How to read the minimal form

  • Requires: follow the arrows upwards. MovementFilter reaches BLEv40 and then the box, so it requires BLEv40, Screen, OLED and CapacityButton.
  • Excludes: a red line also applies to everything below its ends. BT40 conflicts with the box, so it conflicts with whatever points to the box: TouchScreen, BLEv40, BLEv42 and MovementFilter.
  • At least one: a green line also applies to everything above its ends. If every band has A or B, and A requires C, then every band has C or B.

The figure puts the minimal form of the three graphs in one drawing.

The whole model in one picture: dependencies (blue arrows), conflicts (dashed red) and “at least one” (dotted green), all in minimal form.

Nothing is lost: vp_expand()

The minimal form is not an approximation. vp_expand() rebuilds the complete graphs from it, and vp_read() reads the minimal form that vp_generate() wrote:

written <- vp_read("out/miband3_realized", form = "minimal")
rebuilt <- vp_expand(written)
identical(rebuilt$requires, band$requires)
#> [1] TRUE
identical(rebuilt$excludes, band$excludes)
#> [1] TRUE
identical(rebuilt$atleastone, band$atleastone)
#> [1] TRUE

Keep the minimal form to look at and to draw. Keep the complete graphs to compute with. They say the same.

For this small model the saving is modest. For the Linux kernel (version 3.13) the complete graphs have 145,685 links and the minimal form 11,981.

The kernel: “can these go together?”

The question

Suppose you make these bands. Customers, or your marketing department, come to you with wish lists:

  • “a band with a touch screen, a heart-rate sensor and NFC”;
  • “a band with a movement filter and Bluetooth 4.2”;
  • “a band with a touch screen and classic Bluetooth”.

In the language of software product lines, a wish list is a partial configuration Czarnecki et al. (2005); Benavides et al. (2010): a configuration in which some features have been decided and the others are still open (a wish list decides only features that a product must have; a partial configuration can also say which ones it must not have). Which of them can be built? A wish list can be built when at least one valid configuration has all its features. The Mi Band 3 has 11 features that can vary, so there are 2,048 different wish lists, and only 520 of them can be built. Checking them one by one against the 24 valid configurations is tedious; for Linux, whose configurations cannot even be counted, it is impossible.

The graphs of the previous sections already hold the answer: a wish list can be built exactly when no two of its features exclude each other, directly or through what they bring along (with one limit, Limits and theory). vp_can_go_together() checks it:

vp_can_go_together(
  band,
  list(
    c("TouchScreen", "HeartRateSensor", "NFC"),
    c("MovementFilter", "BLEv42"),
    c("TouchScreen", "BT40")
  )
)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 3
#>   wish                              possible reasons                                                
#>   <chr>                             <lgl>    <chr>                                                  
#> 1 TouchScreen, HeartRateSensor, NFC TRUE     ""                                                     
#> 2 MovementFilter, BLEv42            FALSE    "MovementFilter excludes BLEv42 (which brings HeartRat~
#> 3 TouchScreen, BT40                 FALSE    "TouchScreen (which brings Screen) excludes BT40"

But the graphs hold much more than this question needs: for Linux 3.13, 7,100 configuration options and 145,685 links. The kernel is a much smaller map that keeps only what this one question needs. It adapts the co-installability kernels of software packages Vouillon and Di Cosmo (2013).

The kernel is a map made for one question: “can these features be in the same product?”. It keeps the features that can make the answer “no”, with the links between them, and puts all the other features into a single box.

How the kernel is made

Three simplifications turn the graphs into the kernel. Follow them on the figure, which paints every feature with the colour of the box it will end up in.

1. Features that always go together count as one. The 3 features of the atomic set (Screen, OLED and CapacityButton) are always selected together, so for any wish list they stand or fall together. They become one box, A (blue).

2. Features that can never cause trouble are set aside. A feature is trouble-free when it excludes no other feature, neither by itself nor through the features it brings along. NFC is trouble-free: it excludes nothing. ContactlessPayment brings NFC along, and excludes nothing either. Adding them to a wish list can never make it impossible, so for this question they can be forgotten. All the trouble-free features go into one single box, the class “can always be added”, C (green).

Having no red line of your own is not enough to be trouble-free. TouchScreen excludes nothing by itself, but it brings Screen along, and Screen excludes BT40: a band with a touch screen can never use classic Bluetooth. So TouchScreen can cause trouble, and it keeps a box of its own, B (orange). So do the other five features that can cause trouble, each with its own colour.

3. Between the boxes, only two kinds of line are kept: the arrows that say which box brings which along, and the red lines of the root conflicts, the primitive conflicts of the minimal form, from which every other conflict follows.

The minimal form, each feature painted with the colour of its box in the kernel. The two green features (C) are trouble-free; each other colour is a feature, or an atomic set, that can cause trouble.

Each box is called a class. vp_kernel() lists the classes and vp_kernel_links() the links between them:

vp_kernel(band)
#> # A tibble: 11 x 4
#>    class label              feature            trouble_free
#>    <int> <chr>              <chr>              <lgl>       
#>  1     1 Screen             Screen             FALSE       
#>  2     1 Screen             OLED               FALSE       
#>  3     1 Screen             CapacityButton     FALSE       
#>  4     2 TouchScreen        TouchScreen        FALSE       
#>  5     3 ContactlessPayment ContactlessPayment TRUE        
#>  6     3 ContactlessPayment NFC                TRUE        
#>  7     4 MovementFilter     MovementFilter     FALSE       
#>  8     5 HeartRateSensor    HeartRateSensor    FALSE       
#>  9     6 BLEv40             BLEv40             FALSE       
#> 10     7 BLEv42             BLEv42             FALSE       
#> 11     8 BT40               BT40               FALSE
vp_kernel_links(band)
#> # A tibble: 9 x 3
#>   from           link     to             
#>   <chr>          <chr>    <chr>          
#> 1 TouchScreen    requires Screen         
#> 2 MovementFilter requires Screen         
#> 3 MovementFilter requires BLEv40         
#> 4 BLEv40         requires Screen         
#> 5 BLEv42         requires Screen         
#> 6 BLEv42         requires HeartRateSensor
#> 7 Screen         excludes BT40           
#> 8 MovementFilter excludes HeartRateSensor
#> 9 BLEv40         excludes BLEv42
The kernel of the Mi Band 3: each box is a class, named in the drawing with the letters used in the text.

The 11 features, 21 arrows and 10 conflicts of the graphs became 8 boxes, 6 arrows and 3 red lines. Three red lines are enough because every conflict of the band comes from one of three root conflicts: a screen against classic Bluetooth (A–H), the movement filter against the heart-rate sensor (D–E), and the two versions of BLE against each other (F–G). The arrows carry them to other features: D (MovementFilter) points to F (BLEv40), which conflicts with G (BLEv42), so the movement filter conflicts with BLEv42 too.

Reading the kernel

What you see Where it is What it means
a box a class of vp_kernel(); a line of __kernel_classes.txt one or more features that count as one when you ask “can these go together?”
the green box the class with trouble_free TRUE features that can be added to any wish list
an arrow A → B a requires row of vp_kernel_links(); __kernel_requires.net every product with A has B too: A brings B along, and with it the conflicts of B
a red line A — B an excludes row of vp_kernel_links(); __kernel_excludes.net a root conflict: no product has A and B together

And this is the whole recipe for the question:

To know whether a wish list can be built:

  1. replace each feature by its box, and forget the green box;
  2. add every box that your boxes point to (the arrows already include whatever a box brings along indirectly, so one step is enough);
  3. look at the red lines: if one of them joins two of your boxes, the wish list cannot be built, and that red line says why; if none does, it can.

Three wish lists

“A touch screen, a heart-rate sensor and NFC.” TouchScreen is in box B, HeartRateSensor in E, NFC in the green box C, which we forget. B points to A: a touch screen brings the screen along. The boxes are B, E and A, and no red line joins two of them. It can be built.

“A touch screen, a heart-rate sensor and NFC” on the kernel. Thick borders: the boxes of the wished features. Dashed border: a box they bring along (thick blue arrow). Grey: the boxes that play no part. No red line joins two of the coloured boxes: the wish list can be built.

“A movement filter and Bluetooth 4.2.” D points to A and F; G points to A and E. Among D, G, A, F and E there are two red lines. D–E: the movement filter excludes the heart-rate sensor, which Bluetooth 4.2 needs. F–G: the movement filter needs BLE version 4.0, and a band has only one version. It cannot be built, for two reasons.

“A movement filter and Bluetooth 4.2”: the two thick red lines join boxes of the wish list. It cannot be built.

“A touch screen and classic Bluetooth.” B points to A, and a red line joins A and H. It cannot be built: a touch screen needs a screen, and a band with classic Bluetooth has none.

“A touch screen and classic Bluetooth”: the touch screen brings the screen along, and the screen excludes classic Bluetooth.

This recipe was checked against the 24 valid configurations of the band, for all 2,048 wish lists: the kernel gives the right answer every time (520 can be built, 1,528 cannot).

What the kernel is good for

  1. Answering “can these go together?” with a small map. A configurator, a sales tool or a planning spreadsheet can keep the kernel instead of the whole graphs and check any wish list in the three steps above. For the Mi Band the saving is small. For Linux 3.13 the kernel has 1,205 classes, 3,393 arrows and 578 red lines, instead of 7,100 options and 145,685 links.
  2. Knowing which features are free extras. The green class lists the features that can be offered with any product, whatever else is chosen. In Linux 3.13 it holds 5,733 of the 7,100 configuration options that can vary (81 %): only 1,367 options, in 1,204 classes, can ever make a selection impossible.
  3. Knowing where the trouble comes from. The red lines are the root conflicts, and the arrows show how they spread. In the Mi Band, 3 root conflicts explain all 10 conflicts of the excludes graph.
  4. Measuring how entangled a product line is, and what a change did to it. The planned version of the Mi Band 3 (Comparing versions) has only one cross-tree constraint. Its kernel has 4 classes, and its green class holds 8 features:
planned <- vp_generate(
  vp_example("miband3_planned.uvl"),
  or_graph = TRUE,
  kernel = TRUE
)
vp_kernel(planned) |> filter(trouble_free)
#> # A tibble: 8 x 4
#>   class label  feature            trouble_free
#>   <int> <chr>  <chr>              <lgl>       
#> 1     1 Screen Screen             TRUE        
#> 2     1 Screen OLED               TRUE        
#> 3     1 Screen CapacityButton     TRUE        
#> 4     1 Screen TouchScreen        TRUE        
#> 5     1 Screen ContactlessPayment TRUE        
#> 6     1 Screen MovementFilter     TRUE        
#> 7     1 Screen HeartRateSensor    TRUE        
#> 8     1 Screen NFC                TRUE
The kernel of the planned Mi Band 3: 4 classes. The green box holds 8 trouble-free features; in the realized band only 2 of them are left.

The four cross-tree constraints added in the realized band made 6 of these features able to cause trouble. A kernel that grows means features that interact more; a green class that shrinks means fewer free extras.

The three files

With kernel = TRUE, vp_generate() also writes the kernel. The first file lists the classes, one per line; the other two are graphs like those of the previous sections, but their dots are the classes, not the features (vertex 1 is the first class, and so on; each class is named after its first member):

show_file("kernel_classes.txt")
#> Screen   OLED    CapacityButton
#> TouchScreen
#> ContactlessPayment   NFC
#> MovementFilter
#> HeartRateSensor
#> BLEv40
#> BLEv42
#> BT40
show_file("kernel_requires.net")
#> *Vertices 8
#> 1 "Screen"
#> 2 "TouchScreen"
#> 3 "ContactlessPayment"
#> 4 "MovementFilter"
#> 5 "HeartRateSensor"
#> 6 "BLEv40"
#> 7 "BLEv42"
#> 8 "BT40"
#> *Arcs
#> 2 1
#> 4 1
#> 4 6
#> 6 1
#> 7 1
#> 7 5
show_file("kernel_excludes.net")
#> *Vertices 8
#> 1 "Screen"
#> 2 "TouchScreen"
#> 3 "ContactlessPayment"
#> 4 "MovementFilter"
#> 5 "HeartRateSensor"
#> 6 "BLEv40"
#> 7 "BLEv42"
#> 8 "BT40"
#> *Edges
#> 1 8
#> 4 5
#> 6 7

What the kernel is not

A class is not an atomic set. The members of an atomic set, like the 3 features of box A, are always selected together. The members of a class merely behave alike for this question: the two features of the green box share a class, yet a band can have NFC without ContactlessPayment.

Only rules about two features. The kernel, like the graphs, is built from relationships between two features, and a rule that ties three or more features at once is invisible to it. So a “no” of the kernel is always right, but a “yes” can be wrong. Limits and theory shows when, how often, and how to be sure.

The kernel also only deals with features that you want; what follows from leaving a feature out is the business of the at-least-one graph, which the kernel does not use (vp_partial_configuration() and vp_consequences() use it).

For the curious: the recipe of the program. It starts from the graph in which each atomic set is one node, and from the root conflicts. It deletes every arrow that points to a node that excludes nothing; gives each node the set of nodes it still requires, itself included if it excludes something; and merges the nodes that have the same set. The trouble-free nodes all get the empty set, which is why they end up in one class.

The two reports: what was decided, and how the run went

Every run writes two files that describe the run itself. A model read by vp_read() or returned by vp_generate() holds both: band$variables and band$summary.

What was decided about each feature: __variables.csv

This file has one line per variable of the formula. It opens in any spreadsheet, and in R it is a tibble:

print(band$variables, n = Inf)
#> # A tibble: 24 x 8
#>    dimacs_var name               output_name        node_id class    status   decision rule 
#>         <int> <chr>              <chr>                <int> <chr>    <chr>    <chr>    <chr>
#>  1          1 SmartWatch         <NA>                    NA ABSTRACT core     dropped  U4   
#>  2          2 Screen             Screen                   1 OPTION   variable kept     U5   
#>  3          3 TouchScreen        TouchScreen              2 OPTION   variable kept     U5   
#>  4          4 OLED               OLED                     3 OPTION   variable kept     U5   
#>  5          5 CapacityButton     CapacityButton           4 OPTION   variable kept     U5   
#>  6          6 Functionalities    <NA>                    NA ABSTRACT core     dropped  U4   
#>  7          7 FitnessMonitor     FitnessMonitor          NA OPTION   core     kept     U5   
#>  8          8 SleepTracker       SleepTracker            NA OPTION   core     kept     U5   
#>  9          9 VibrateAlert       VibrateAlert            NA OPTION   core     kept     U5   
#> 10         10 Call               Call                    NA OPTION   core     kept     U5   
#> 11         11 Notification       Notification            NA OPTION   core     kept     U5   
#> 12         12 ContactlessPayment ContactlessPayment       5 OPTION   variable kept     U5   
#> 13         13 Sensors            <NA>                    NA ABSTRACT core     dropped  U4   
#> 14         14 Pedometer          Pedometer               NA OPTION   core     kept     U5   
#> 15         15 MovementFilter     MovementFilter           6 OPTION   variable kept     U5   
#> 16         16 Accelerometer      Accelerometer           NA OPTION   core     kept     U5   
#> 17         17 HeartRateSensor    HeartRateSensor          7 OPTION   variable kept     U5   
#> 18         18 Connectivity       <NA>                    NA ABSTRACT core     dropped  U4   
#> 19         19 Bluetooth          Bluetooth               NA OPTION   core     kept     U5   
#> 20         20 BLE                <NA>                    NA ABSTRACT variable dropped  U4   
#> 21         21 BLEv40             BLEv40                   8 OPTION   variable kept     U5   
#> 22         22 BLEv42             BLEv42                   9 OPTION   variable kept     U5   
#> 23         23 BT40               BT40                    10 OPTION   variable kept     U5   
#> 24         24 NFC                NFC                     11 OPTION   variable kept     U5
Column Meaning
dimacs_var The number of the variable in the formula.
name Its name in the model.
output_name Its name in the graphs and lists. In this model it is always the same as name; the example below shows when it differs. Empty if the variable is not kept.
node_id Its number in the graphs. Empty if it is not a dot of the graphs: here, the core features and the abstract ones, which are dropped.
class What it is. Here OPTION (an ordinary feature; remember that the engine says option) or ABSTRACT (an abstract feature, the root included). A root that is not abstract is ROOT.
status How it behaves: core, dead or variable.
decision What was done with it: kept, dropped or merged_into: another. Here the abstract features are dropped and all the others are kept.
rule Why: the name of the rule that decided. Here U4 or U5: see the table below.

The rules of a UVL model. Each kind of formula has its own set of rules (Formulas made by other tools). For a formula translated from UVL by variplex itself there are five, and they are simple, because the translator marks in the formula, with special comments, which variable is the root, which features are abstract, and which variables are helpers that it added (Looking at the formula shows these comments):

Rule It applies to class decision In the Mi Band 3
U1 a helper variable of the Tseitin transformation (tseitin = TRUE), marked c aux N tseitin TSEITIN dropped none; 10 with tseitin = TRUE
U2 a helper variable that splits a long clause, marked c aux N chain (written by older versions of the translator) CHAIN dropped none
U3 the root of the feature tree, marked c root N, if it is not abstract ROOT kept (it is core) none: the root, SmartWatch, is abstract
U4 a feature marked {abstract}, marked c abstract N; the root too, if it is abstract ABSTRACT dropped (abstract = "keep" keeps them, abstract = "merge" merges them) 5: SmartWatch, Functionalities, Sensors, Connectivity, BLE
U5 every other feature OPTION kept the other 19

So, in the report above, the abstract features, the root SmartWatch among them, are dropped by U4, and every other feature is kept by U5. With tseitin = TRUE the formula also has helper variables, and their rows say that U1 dropped them:

tseitin <- vp_generate(vp_example("miband3_realized.uvl"), tseitin = TRUE)
tseitin$variables |> filter(rule == "U1") |> head(3)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 8
#>   dimacs_var name  output_name node_id class   status   decision rule 
#>        <int> <chr> <chr>         <int> <chr>   <chr>    <chr>    <chr>
#> 1         25 <NA>  <NA>             NA TSEITIN variable dropped  U1   
#> 2         26 <NA>  <NA>             NA TSEITIN variable dropped  U1   
#> 3         27 <NA>  <NA>             NA TSEITIN core     dropped  U1

An example of output_name. In a UVL model, a feature keeps its name. Formulas made by other tools sometimes write the names of the options with a prefix that is not part of the name. KconfigSampler, for instance, puts the type of each option in front of it: the option CONFIG_PLATFORM_WIN32 of the library axTLS is the variable boolean_CONFIG_PLATFORM_WIN32 of its formula, and variplex shows it under its real name. Three rows of the report of that formula (from the dataset of Strong4VM):

dimacs_var,name,output_name,node_id,class,status,decision,rule
2,boolean_CONFIG_PLATFORM_WIN32,CONFIG_PLATFORM_WIN32,1,OPTION,variable,kept,S2
10,int_CONFIG_X509_MAX_CA_CERTS_EQ_3,,,VALUE,variable,dropped,S5
14,ART_1,,,TSEITIN,variable,dropped,S1

The first row is the option: name is the variable of the formula, output_name the name in the graphs. The other two are helper variables of the translation (the value 3 of a number option, and a Tseitin variable), which are dropped, so their output_name is empty.

For a UVL model this report is simple: every feature is kept but the abstract ones. It becomes essential for formulas produced by other tools, which are full of variables that are not features (Formulas made by other tools). There, this report is where you check that variplex kept the right ones. vp_classify() writes it without computing any graph, which is fast even for Linux.

Try it

Is a feature missing from a graph? Look at its row. If status is core or dead, it is in the corresponding list instead. If decision is dropped, the column rule tells which rule dropped it.

A summary of the run: __summary.json

The second report is a JSON file, a format that people can read and programs can load. It records how the run was made and what it found; in R it is a list:

names(band$summary)

#>  [5] "input"             "counts"            "kernel"            "mig"              
#>  [9] "uvl"               "checks"            "warnings"          "timings"
str(band$summary$counts)

#>   .. ..$ kept   : int 0

#>   .. ..$ kept   : int 19
#>   .. ..$ dropped: int 0
#>   .. ..$ merged : int 0
#>  $ formula_variables      : int 24
#>  $ fresh_variables        : int 0
#>  $ kept                   : int 19
#>  $ dropped                : int 5
#>  $ merged                 : int 0
#>  $ core                   : int 8
#>  $ dead                   : int 0
#>  $ variable_options       : int 11
#>  $ unconstrained          : int 0
#>  $ nodes                  : int 11
#>  $ arcs                   : int 21
#>  $ edges                  : int 10
#>  $ atleastone_edges       : int 3

#>  $ kernel_nodes           : int 8

#>  $ skeleton_arcs          : int 6

#>  $ primitive_atleastone   : int 1

  • input: the size of the formula and the translator profile, with how it was chosen (here, from the .uvl extension).
  • uvl: facts about the UVL model: its features, how many are abstract, and how many constraints had to be skipped because they are not logical (none here).
  • counts: the numbers of this vignette in one place: core, dead, nodes, arcs, edges, atomic sets, links of the minimal form, classes of the kernel, and calls to the solver (solver_calls, fewer than the questions when the MIG answers some of them alone: Where the time went).
  • checks: whether the results passed the consistency checks of Is everything consistent?.
  • warnings: everything the run warned about.

The summary also has every option with the value that was used, also those you did not give, the command line that the options make (command_line), and the time spent in each step. With it, a result can always be traced back to how it was produced.

Where the time went: timings and mig

The times are in two places of the summary, in seconds. On the model of the vignettes they are all close to zero, so here is a larger one, the automotive product line automotive01 of the examples of Strong4VM, run with four threads (threads = 4):

"timings": { "parse": 0.13, "classify": 0.02, "backbone": 0.34, "main_loop": 1.43, "atomic": 0.01,
             "post_processing": 0.25, "write": 0.08, "checks": 0.10 },
"mig": { "jobs": 2513, "jobs_without_solver": 1690, "solver_calls": 1123,
         "timings": { "build": 0.004, "setup": 0.05, "jobs": 1.37,
                      "graph_thread_seconds": 0.63, "filter_thread_seconds": 1.35, "solver_thread_seconds": 3.11 } }

timings has one entry per step of the run, one after the other: reading the model (parse), sorting its variables (classify), finding the core and dead features (backbone), asking about each feature that can vary (main_loop), the atomic sets (atomic), the minimal form and the kernel (post_processing), writing the files (write) and the consistency checks (checks). On large models the main loop is usually the largest part; on a small model, or on a slow disk, writing the files can take as long.

The main loop does not send every question to the solver. First it looks at a modal implication graph (MIG): a cheap picture of the clauses of the formula, from which many answers can be read without a solver, and which tells which features a selection cannot affect. Only what is left goes to the backbone solver. The graphs are the same with and without it (mig = FALSE switches it off); only the time changes. mig$timings splits the main loop into its parts:

Entry What it measures
build Creating the MIG, once, before the threads start
setup Creating one solver per thread
jobs The questions, from the first to the last: wall-clock time, like the entries of timings
graph_thread_seconds Using the MIG: following its edges from the selected feature
filter_thread_seconds Using the MIG: choosing what to ask, and ruling out answers with the products the solver already found
solver_thread_seconds Calling the backbone solver

The last three entries are thread time: the time of every thread, added up. With four threads they can add up to about four times jobs. Do not add them to the wall-clock entries; compare them with one another. With quiet = FALSE, a run that used the MIG ends with these numbers already put together, with their shares, as the first run of Get started shows: total run for the total, calling the backbone solver for the solver (with before the main loop, which holds the core and dead features), and create the MIG with propagation and weak reach and candidates and witnesses for the MIG.

Checking and explaining

Two questions about the results need no solver: are they consistent, and where does a relationship come from?

Is everything consistent? vp_check() 

vp_check(band)
#> # A tibble: 6 x 3
#>   property                                                           holds violations
#>   <chr>                                                              <lgl>      <int>
#> 1 requires is complete: A -> B and B -> C give A -> C                TRUE           0
#> 2 conflicts are inherited: A -> B and B excludes C give A excludes C TRUE           0
#> 3 no feature requires two features that exclude each other           TRUE           0
#> 4 no pair both requires and excludes                                 TRUE           0
#> 5 at-least-one is inherited upwards: A or B, and B -> C give A or C  TRUE           0
#> 6 A excludes B and (B or C) give A -> C                              TRUE           0

vp_check() verifies properties that any correct result must have: if A requires B and B requires C, the arrow from A to C must be there; a conflict of B must also be a conflict of everything that requires B; no feature may require two features that exclude each other (it would be dead). A run of vp_generate() already does these checks before it ends (and stops with an error if one fails, unless fail_on_check = FALSE). The function is useful for graphs that come from somewhere else, or that someone may have edited.

Why? vp_explain_conflict() and vp_explain_requires()

The graphs say that two features are in conflict. The explanations say why. Explaining implicit relationships by what they come from has been studied for feature models Kowal et al. (2016); Ananieva et al. (2016); Duszynski et al. (2019); these functions do it with the graphs alone:

vp_explain_conflict(band, "MovementFilter", "BT40")
#> # A tibble: 3 x 5
#>   origin  step from           link     to    
#>    <int> <int> <chr>          <chr>    <chr> 
#> 1      1     1 MovementFilter requires BLEv40
#> 2      1     2 BLEv40         requires Screen
#> 3      1     3 Screen         excludes BT40

Read it like this: the conflict between MovementFilter and BT40 is inherited. Its origin is the primitive conflict between Screen and BT40, and MovementFilter gets it through the chain MovementFilter → BLEv40 → Screen. The figure highlights that path.

The explanation of a conflict. MovementFilter leads to Screen through the thick blue arrows, and Screen has a conflict of its own with BT40 (thick red line). The pale links play no part in it.

If the conflict is one of the primitive ones, there is nothing behind it:

vp_explain_conflict(band, "Screen", "BT40")
#> # A tibble: 1 x 5
#>   origin  step from   link     to   
#>    <int> <int> <chr>  <chr>    <chr>
#> 1      1     1 Screen excludes BT40

The same works for a dependency:

vp_explain_requires(band, "MovementFilter", "Screen")
#> # A tibble: 4 x 5
#>   route  step from           link       to    
#>   <int> <int> <chr>          <chr>      <chr> 
#> 1     1     1 MovementFilter requires   BLEv40
#> 2     1     2 BLEv40         requires   Screen
#> 3     2     1 MovementFilter excludes   BT40  
#> 4     2     2 BT40           atleastone Screen

The second route appears because this model has the at-least-one graph: MovementFilter excludes BT40, and every band has BT40 or a screen, so a band with the movement filter has a screen. Two different reasons for the same fact. And if the relationship does not hold, you are told so:

vp_explain_requires(band, "TouchScreen", "HeartRateSensor")
#> "TouchScreen" does not require "HeartRateSensor": some valid product has TouchScreen without HeartRateSensor.
#> # A tibble: 0 x 5
#> # i 5 variables: route <int>, step <int>, from <chr>, link <chr>, to <chr>

Comparing versions

Models change. A new version adds features and constraints, and the question is what that did to the relationships Thüm et al. (2009); Acher et al. (2012). This section compares two versions of the same band, as planned and as built, and then a whole chain of versions: seven generations of the Mi Band. The vignette Following a model through time goes much further.

Two versions: the band as planned and as built

The examples also have miband3_planned.uvl: the Mi Band 3 as it was planned. It has the same 24 features, but only 1 of the 5 cross-tree constraints. The realized model, our example, adds these 4:

constraints <- function(file) {
  l <- trimws(readLines(file))
  l[(which(l == "constraints") + 1):length(l)]
}
setdiff(
  constraints(vp_example("miband3_realized.uvl")),
  constraints(vp_example("miband3_planned.uvl"))
)
#> [1] "MovementFilter => !HeartRateSensor & BLEv40" "BLE => HeartRateSensor | MovementFilter"    
#> [3] "!Screen => BT40"                             "BT40 => !Screen"

The planned band (computed in the kernel above) has only 10 dependencies and 3 conflicts:

planned
#> variplex model "miband3_planned"
#>   features: 11 variable (the nodes of the graphs), 8 core, 0 dead
#>   requires: 10 arrows   excludes: 3 lines
#>   at least one: 0 lines
#>   atomic sets: 1 (of two or more features)
The planned Mi Band 3: 10 dependencies (arrows) and 3 conflicts (dashed lines).

Now compare the two. vp_compare() takes the old version and the new one, and gives one row per graph:

vp_compare(planned, band)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 10
#>   graph       kept added removed old_links new_links gained  lost jaccard spearman
#>   <chr>      <int> <int>   <int>     <int>     <int>  <int> <int>   <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 requires      11     0       0        10        21     11     0   0.476    0.867
#> 2 excludes      11     0       0         3        10      7     0   0.3     NA    
#> 3 atleastone    11     0       0         0         3      3     0   0       NA
  • kept, added, removed: the comparison is about the features that can vary, and both versions have the same
  • requires: 11 dependencies were gained and none was lost. The four new cross-tree constraints created 11 “requires” relationships.
  • excludes: 7 conflicts were gained.
  • atleastone: 3 “at least one” edges were gained. This row appears because both versions have the at-least-one graph.
  • jaccard and spearman measure how much stayed the same: see below.
What changed from the planned band to the realized one. Green: the 11 dependencies (arrows) and 7 conflicts (dashed lines) that only the realized band has. Grey: what the planned band already had. Nothing was lost, so nothing is purple.

The two measures. jaccard is the links in both versions divided by the links in either: 1 when the graph did not change, 0 when nothing of it is left. With the numbers of the dependencies: the planned band has 10 and the realized one 21. None was lost, so all 10 of the planned band are in both, and 11 were gained: 10/21 = 0.47619. For the conflicts it is 3/10 = 0.30, and for the “at least one” edges 0/3 = 0.00. spearman sorts the kept features by how many features require them, in each version, and compares the two orders: 1 for the same order. A Spearman of 0.87 says that the features that the others depend on most are almost the same in both versions: the new constraints added links, but did not move the centre of the model.

vp_changed_links() lists the links that changed, and vp_state_moves() the features that moved between core, dead and variable (none here):

vp_changed_links(planned, band, "requires")
#> # A tibble: 11 x 3
#>    from           to              change
#>    <chr>          <chr>           <chr> 
#>  1 MovementFilter Screen          gained
#>  2 MovementFilter OLED            gained
#>  3 MovementFilter CapacityButton  gained
#>  4 MovementFilter BLEv40          gained
#>  5 BLEv40         Screen          gained
#>  6 BLEv40         OLED            gained
#>  7 BLEv40         CapacityButton  gained
#>  8 BLEv42         Screen          gained
#>  9 BLEv42         OLED            gained
#> 10 BLEv42         CapacityButton  gained
#> 11 BLEv42         HeartRateSensor gained
vp_state_moves(planned, band)
#> # A tibble: 0 x 3
#> # i 3 variables: feature <chr>, before <chr>, after <chr>

Four cross-tree constraints, 11 new dependencies and 7 new conflicts. A comparison of the graphs measures the real effect of a change, which is rarely the size of the change.

A feature that changed its name

Versions are compared by the names of the features. Suppose that in the planned band the first version of Bluetooth Low Energy was called BLEv40Old (the example miband3_planned_old.uvl). Compared as they are, the two versions look as if one feature had been removed and another added, and since links are compared only among the features of both versions, the links of that feature drop out of the comparison (7 dependencies gained instead of 11):

planned_old <- vp_generate(
  vp_example("miband3_planned_old.uvl"),
  or_graph = TRUE
)
vp_compare(planned_old, band) |>
  select(graph, kept, added, removed, gained, lost)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 6
#>   graph       kept added removed gained  lost
#>   <chr>      <int> <int>   <int>  <int> <int>
#> 1 requires      10     1       1      7     0
#> 2 excludes      10     1       1      7     0
#> 3 atleastone    10     1       1      3     0

vp_rename() gives the features of the old version their new names first: from a named vector, or from a file with one rename per line, the old name, a space, and the new name (a tab instead of the space if a name has spaces of its own; lines that start with # and empty lines are ignored). With it, the comparison is the one above:

vp_compare(vp_rename(planned_old, c(BLEv40Old = "BLEv40")), band) |>
  select(graph, kept, added, removed, gained, lost)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 6
#>   graph       kept added removed gained  lost
#>   <chr>      <int> <int>   <int>  <int> <int>
#> 1 requires      11     0       0     11     0
#> 2 excludes      11     0       0      7     0
#> 3 atleastone    11     0       0      3     0
cat(readLines(vp_example("miband3_renames.txt")), sep = "\n")
#> # one rename per line: the old name, a space (a tab if a name has spaces), the new name
#> BLEv40Old BLEv40
vp_compare(vp_rename(planned_old, vp_example("miband3_renames.txt")), band) |>
  select(graph, kept, gained, lost)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 4
#>   graph       kept gained  lost
#>   <chr>      <int>  <int> <int>
#> 1 requires      11     11     0
#> 2 excludes      11      7     0
#> 3 atleastone    11      3     0

A rename whose old name is not a feature of the model changes nothing, so vp_rename() warns about it. vp_rename_candidates() finds the likely renames by comparing the links of the features that disappeared and appeared.

Many versions: seven generations of the band

A product line lives for years, and each new product is a new version of its model Lotufo et al. (2010); Kuiter et al. (2026). The examples have the realized model of 7 generations of the band: the Mi Band 1, 1s, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 (there is no realized model of the Mi Band 5 or 7). vp_history() runs every version and gathers the models, oldest first:

gens <- c(
  "miband1",
  "miband1s",
  "miband2",
  "miband3",
  "miband4",
  "miband6",
  "miband8"
)
history <- vp_history(
  vp_example(paste0(gens, "_realized.uvl")),
  versions = gens,
  or_graph = TRUE
)
history
#> # A tibble: 7 x 2
#>   version  model     
#>   <fct>    <list>    
#> 1 miband1  <vp_model>
#> 2 miband1s <vp_model>
#> 3 miband2  <vp_model>
#> 4 miband3  <vp_model>
#> 5 miband4  <vp_model>
#> 6 miband6  <vp_model>
#> 7 miband8  <vp_model>
vp_history_sizes(history) |>
  select(version, features, core, requires, excludes, atleastone)
#> # A tibble: 7 x 6
#>   version  features  core requires excludes atleastone
#>   <fct>       <int> <int>    <int>    <int>      <int>
#> 1 miband1         0     8        0        0          0
#> 2 miband1s        1     8        0        0          0
#> 3 miband2         8     8        6        3          0
#> 4 miband3        11     8       21       10          3
#> 5 miband4        17     8       32       35          1
#> 6 miband6        21     8      108       72          1
#> 7 miband8        23     8      127       93          1
  • The first band offers no choice at all: its 8 features are all core (and its 4 abstract features are left out). There is exactly one product, and nothing to draw.
  • Every generation adds features that can vary: 0 in the Mi Band 1, 23 in the Mi Band 8. The number of core features stays at 8.
  • The relationships grow much faster than the constraints. The Mi Band 8 has 22 cross-tree constraints, and variplex finds 127 dependencies and 93 conflicts among its 23 features that can vary: the lesson of the requires graph, once more.

vp_history_changes() compares each version with the one before:

vp_history_changes(history) |>
  filter(graph == "requires") |>
  select(from, to, kept, added, removed, gained, lost, jaccard, spearman)
#> # A tibble: 6 x 9
#>   from     to        kept added removed gained  lost jaccard spearman
#>   <fct>    <fct>    <int> <int>   <int>  <int> <int>   <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 miband1  miband1s     0     1       0      0     0   1       NA    
#> 2 miband1s miband2      1     7       0      0     0   1       NA    
#> 3 miband2  miband3      8     3       0     11     0   0.353    0.894
#> 4 miband3  miband4     11     6       0     11    10   0.344    0.297
#> 5 miband4  miband6     17     4       0     45     4   0.364    0.302
#> 6 miband6  miband8     21     2       0      9     8   0.855    0.864

What is compared

The comparison is about the features that can vary in both versions: the kept features. In the first step, from the Mi Band 1 to the Mi Band 1s, none is kept, because the Mi Band 1 has no feature that can vary. Core features are not vertices of the graphs, so they are not counted as kept, even when both versions have them; vp_state_moves() follows them instead. The step from the Mi Band 1s to the Mi Band 2:

vp_state_moves(history$model[[2]], history$model[[3]])
#> # A tibble: 8 x 3
#>   feature        before after   
#>   <chr>          <chr>  <chr>   
#> 1 BT40           core   variable
#> 2 Screen         absent variable
#> 3 OLED           absent variable
#> 4 CapacityButton absent variable
#> 5 MovementFilter absent variable
#> 6 BLEv40         absent variable
#> 7 BLEv42         absent variable
#> 8 Bluetooth      absent core

The rows whose state before is absent are the new features. The row of BT40 is a move: classic Bluetooth was core in the Mi Band 1s (every band had it) and can vary in the Mi Band 2, where a band has either classic Bluetooth or BLE. The new feature Bluetooth is core: every band has one of the two.

The relationships are compared only among the kept features. A link that touches a new feature is not counted as gained: it could not exist before. So the step from the Mi Band 1s to the Mi Band 2 has nothing to compare: with only 1 kept feature, there is no link to compare, and its Jaccard of 1 is a convention, not “no change”. Always look at the number of kept features first.

A redesign: the Mi Band 3 to the Mi Band 4 

m3 <- history$model[[4]]
m4 <- history$model[[5]]
vp_compare(m3, m4) |>
  select(graph, kept, added, gained, lost, jaccard, spearman)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 7
#>   graph       kept added gained  lost jaccard spearman
#>   <chr>      <int> <int>  <int> <int>   <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 requires      11     6     11    10   0.344    0.297
#> 2 excludes      11     6      8     0   0.556   NA    
#> 3 atleastone    11     6      0     2   0.333   NA

The two versions share 11 features that can vary. Among them, the Mi Band 3 has 21 dependencies and the Mi Band 4 has 22: 11 are in both, 10 were lost and 11 were gained. Notice that 21 and 22 are almost the same number: counting links would say that nothing happened. Jaccard says that more than half of the links are different. The figure draws the three groups on the shared features.

The dependencies among the features that the Mi Band 3 and the Mi Band 4 share. Pale: in both versions. Purple: only in the Mi Band 3, lost. Green: only in the Mi Band 4, gained.

The lost arrows tell one story: every one of them points to OLED or to CapacityButton. In the Mi Band 3, a band with a screen has an OLED screen with a capacity button. The Mi Band 4 brings a second kind of screen, AMOLED: a screen no longer means OLED.

vp_changed_links(m3, m4, "requires") |> filter(change == "lost")
#> # A tibble: 10 x 3
#>    from           to             change
#>    <chr>          <chr>          <chr> 
#>  1 Screen         OLED           lost  
#>  2 Screen         CapacityButton lost  
#>  3 TouchScreen    OLED           lost  
#>  4 TouchScreen    CapacityButton lost  
#>  5 MovementFilter OLED           lost  
#>  6 MovementFilter CapacityButton lost  
#>  7 BLEv40         OLED           lost  
#>  8 BLEv40         CapacityButton lost  
#>  9 BLEv42         OLED           lost  
#> 10 BLEv42         CapacityButton lost

The explanations, asked on each version, confirm it, and they explain one of the gained arrows too:

vp_explain_requires(m3, "Screen", "OLED")
#> # A tibble: 3 x 5
#>   route  step from   link       to   
#>   <int> <int> <chr>  <chr>      <chr>
#> 1     1     1 Screen requires   OLED 
#> 2     2     1 Screen excludes   BT40 
#> 3     2     2 BT40   atleastone OLED
vp_explain_requires(m4, "TouchScreen", "HeartRateSensor")
#> # A tibble: 2 x 5
#>   route  step from        link     to             
#>   <int> <int> <chr>       <chr>    <chr>          
#> 1     1     1 TouchScreen requires BLEv42         
#> 2     1     2 BLEv42      requires HeartRateSensor

In the Mi Band 3 a touch screen did not need a heart-rate sensor (Why? asked the same question). In the Mi Band 4 it does: one of the new constraints, TouchScreen => BLEv42, met an old relationship, BLEv42 requires HeartRateSensor. Nobody wrote “a touch screen needs a heart-rate sensor”; the comparison found it.

Reading a history, step by step

  1. Kept, added, removed. With fewer than two kept features, the Jaccard numbers mean nothing yet.
  2. Jaccard of each graph. Near 1: the relationships among the features you already had stayed as they were. Low: they changed.
  3. Gained and lost. Only gains: the version added rules, and the design got tighter. Losses: something that used to be forced is now a choice.
  4. The names. vp_changed_links() lists every link that changed, vp_state_moves() the new features and the moves. Ask for explanations on both versions for the reasons.
  5. Spearman. Low: the features that everything else depends on are not the same as before.

Using the results in other programs

The graphs are in Pajek format, read by the usual programs for network analysis: Gephi and Pajek (to explore and draw), and the library igraph (to compute; it exists for R, Python and C). The reports are CSV and JSON, read by everything. In R, vp_igraph() gives any graph of a model as an igraph object:

g <- vp_igraph(band, "requires")
sort(igraph::degree(g, mode = "in"), decreasing = TRUE)
#>             Screen               OLED     CapacityButton    HeartRateSensor             BLEv40 
#>                  6                  6                  6                  1                  1 
#>                NFC        TouchScreen ContactlessPayment     MovementFilter             BLEv42 
#>                  1                  0                  0                  0                  0 
#>               BT40 
#>                  0

Counting the arrows that point to a feature tells how many features a change to it can affect, its impact set Abate et al. (2009); measures of this kind, over the whole dataset, are studied in Sánchez et al. (2026). The same, in Python, from the files:

import igraph as ig
g = ig.Graph.Read_Pajek("out/miband3_realized__requires.net")
print(sorted(zip(g.indegree(), g.vs["id"]), reverse=True)[:3])

Pajek has no way to write a double quote inside a name: vp_generate() writes it with a backslash before it, and igraph does not understand that backslash (vp_read() does). No feature of the Mi Band has a double quote in its name; if one of yours does, rename it before you use igraph on the files.

The options of vp_generate()

?vp_generate lists every argument with its default value. The ones you are likely to use:

Argument What it does
output_dir Writes the files in that folder instead of a temporary one.
threads Uses that many threads. For large models this is the difference between minutes and hours. The results are the same with any number.
quiet = FALSE Prints what the run does.
or_graph = TRUE Adds the at-least-one graph (The at-least-one graph).
kernel = TRUE Adds the kernel (The kernel).
representativeness = TRUE Counts, with the model counter GANAK, how many of the products that the graphs let pass are real ones (Measuring your own model).
keep_dimacs = TRUE Keeps the logic formula made from the UVL model.
tseitin = TRUE Uses another way of translating the constraints (the Tseitin transformation), better for very complicated constraints.
fixed_nodes = "keep" Draws the core and dead features in the graphs too.
abstract = "keep" Keeps the abstract features, the root included, which are left out by default.
abstract = "merge" Merges each abstract feature into a feature that is not abstract and is selected in exactly the same products, if there is one.
legacy = TRUE Behaves like version 1 of Strong4VM.
read = FALSE Returns the prefix of the files, without reading them.

vp_classify() only writes the two reports, without computing graphs.

Looking at the formula: keep_dimacs

With keep_dimacs = TRUE (as in the run at the top of this vignette), vp_generate() keeps the logic formula, in a format called DIMACS:

writeLines(readLines("out/miband3_realized.dimacs"))
#> c generated-by uvl2dimacs 2.0 mode=straightforward
#> c Original features: 24
#> c Auxiliary variables: 0
#> c Total variables: 24
#> p cnf 24 47
#> c 1 SmartWatch
#> c 2 Screen
#> c 3 TouchScreen
#> c 4 OLED
#> c 5 CapacityButton
#> c 6 Functionalities
#> c 7 FitnessMonitor
#> c 8 SleepTracker
#> c 9 VibrateAlert
#> c 10 Call
#> c 11 Notification
#> c 12 ContactlessPayment
#> c 13 Sensors
#> c 14 Pedometer
#> c 15 MovementFilter
#> c 16 Accelerometer
#> c 17 HeartRateSensor
#> c 18 Connectivity
#> c 19 Bluetooth
#> c 20 BLE
#> c 21 BLEv40
#> c 22 BLEv42
#> c 23 BT40
#> c 24 NFC
#> c root 1
#> c abstract 1
#> c abstract 6
#> c abstract 13
#> c abstract 18
#> c abstract 20
#> 1 0
#> -2 1 0
#> -1 6 0
#> -6 1 0
#> -1 13 0
#> -13 1 0
#> -1 18 0
#> -18 1 0
#> -3 2 0
#> -2 4 0
#> -4 2 0
#> -4 5 0
#> -5 4 0
#> -6 7 0
#> -7 6 0
#> -6 8 0
#> -8 6 0
#> -6 9 0
#> -9 6 0
#> -12 6 0
#> -9 10 0
#> -10 9 0
#> -9 11 0
#> -11 9 0
#> -13 14 0
#> -14 13 0
#> -13 16 0
#> -16 13 0
#> -17 13 0
#> -15 14 0
#> -18 19 0
#> -19 18 0
#> -24 18 0
#> -19 20 23 0
#> -20 -23 0
#> -20 19 0
#> -23 19 0
#> -20 21 22 0
#> -21 -22 0
#> -21 20 0
#> -22 20 0
#> -15 -17 0
#> -15 21 0
#> -20 17 15 0
#> -12 24 0
#> 2 23 0
#> -23 -2 0

The lines that start with c are comments. Most of them give each feature a number; the last ones mark the root and the abstract features. The line p cnf 24 47 announces 24 variables and 47 clauses. Each of the other lines is one clause: a list of numbers ending in 0, of which at least one must hold. A positive number means “the feature is selected” and a negative one “it is not”. The clause -3 2 0 reads “not TouchScreen, or Screen”: a band with a touch screen has a screen.

With tseitin = TRUE the formula is built differently Kuiter et al. (2022): it gets 10 helper variables (34 in all) and 73 clauses. The graphs are exactly the same; variplex knows that the helpers are not features and leaves them out:

identical(tseitin$requires, band$requires)
#> [1] TRUE

Showing core features and abstract ones

With fixed_nodes = "keep" the graphs also show the core features, 19 features in all. The core ones are isolated dots, and their number in the list is no longer 0:

fixed <- vp_generate(
  vp_example("miband3_realized.uvl"),
  fixed_nodes = "keep",
  read = FALSE
)
head(readLines(paste0(fixed, "__core.txt")), 4)
#> [1] "5 \"FitnessMonitor\"" "6 \"SleepTracker\""   "7 \"VibrateAlert\""   "8 \"Call\""

Abstract features are not parts of a band, so variplex leaves them out. With abstract = "keep" they are kept, the root too: the graphs have 12 features instead of 11 (BLE is abstract and can vary) and the core list has 12 instead of 8. The report shows the decisions:

keep <- vp_generate(vp_example("miband3_realized.uvl"), abstract = "keep")
keep$variables |>
  filter(class == "ABSTRACT") |>
  select(name, output_name, status, decision, rule)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 5
#>   name            output_name     status   decision rule 
#>   <chr>           <chr>           <chr>    <chr>    <chr>
#> 1 SmartWatch      SmartWatch      core     kept     U4   
#> 2 Functionalities Functionalities core     kept     U4   
#> 3 Sensors         Sensors         core     kept     U4   
#> 4 Connectivity    Connectivity    core     kept     U4   
#> 5 BLE             BLE             variable kept     U4

With abstract = "merge" an abstract feature is merged into a feature that is not abstract and is selected in exactly the same bands, if there is one, the way the features of an atomic set are grouped. In this band BLE goes with the screen (the bands with a screen are those with BLE), so it joins the atomic set of Screen; the root and the headings that are in every band, 4 features, join a core feature:

merge <- vp_generate(vp_example("miband3_realized.uvl"), abstract = "merge")
merge$variables |> filter(class == "ABSTRACT") |> select(name, status, decision)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 3
#>   name            status   decision                  
#>   <chr>           <chr>    <chr>                     
#> 1 SmartWatch      core     merged_into:FitnessMonitor
#> 2 Functionalities core     merged_into:FitnessMonitor
#> 3 Sensors         core     merged_into:FitnessMonitor
#> 4 Connectivity    core     merged_into:FitnessMonitor
#> 5 BLE             variable merged_into:Screen

The graphs have 11 features, and nothing is lost: every relationship of BLE is a relationship of Screen. In the planned band no feature goes with BLE, which stands there for the choice “BLEv40 or BLEv42” (Why BLEv40 and BLEv42 are not joined), and abstract = "merge" keeps it. To compare versions, keep the default: with "merge", a feature can appear or disappear from one version to the next only because it became, or stopped being, equivalent to another.

Compatibility with version 1: legacy

Version 1 of Strong4VM wrote four files and treated every variable as a feature. legacy = TRUE reproduces it, for those who need to compare with old results. The graphs then have all 24 features, core ones included, and there is no minimal form:

legacy <- vp_generate(
  vp_example("miband3_realized.uvl"),
  legacy = TRUE,
  read = FALSE
)
#> Warning: 24 variables matched no rule of profile 'generic' and were kept (--unknown-names keep),
#> e.g. SmartWatch, Screen, TouchScreen, OLED, CapacityButton, Functionalities, FitnessMonitor,
#> SleepTracker, VibrateAlert, Call
list.files(dirname(legacy))
#> [1] "miband3_realized__core.txt"      "miband3_realized__dead.txt"     
#> [3] "miband3_realized__excludes.net"  "miband3_realized__requires.net" 
#> [5] "miband3_realized__summary.json"  "miband3_realized__variables.csv"

The warning is version 1 speaking: it had no rules to tell features from other variables, so it kept them all.

Formulas made by other tools

variplex also reads the logic formula of a variability model written in any other language, in DIMACS format, in files ending in .dimacs or .cnf. The translation into a formula is done beforehand by a tool that knows the language: KMax, KConfigReader or KconfigSampler for the Kconfig files of Linux, BusyBox or axTLS, TraVarT for feature models of other notations, and so on. Then, for instance:

linux <- vp_generate("linux.dimacs", threads = 8, or_graph = TRUE)

Such formulas contain many variables that are not features: helpers that the translator invented, encodings of numbers and texts, and so on. In the formula of Linux 3.13 made by KMax, 14,421 of the 23,838 variables are not configuration options. variplex recognises them by rules that depend on the translator, keeps only the real options, and writes its decision for every variable in __variables.csv, with the rule that decided (The two reports shows the rules of a UVL model, and a row of a formula made by KconfigSampler). The translator is detected from the comments of the formula; the argument translator names it if needed, and the arguments tristate, nonbool, visibility, abstract_groups, synthetic_root, unnamed, unknown_names, decls, keep_pattern, drop_pattern and drop_names adjust the rules (?vp_generate). Try them with vp_classify(), which classifies the variables in seconds, before a long run:

vp_classify(vp_example("eleven_options.dimacs"), translator = "kmax")
#> # A tibble: 11 x 8
#>    dimacs_var name             output_name      node_id class  status decision rule 
#>         <int> <chr>            <chr>            <lgl>   <chr>  <lgl>  <chr>    <chr>
#>  1          1 ACPI             ACPI             NA      OPTION NA     kept     K6   
#>  2          2 IA64             IA64             NA      OPTION NA     kept     K6   
#>  3          3 ACPI_INTERPRETER ACPI_INTERPRETER NA      OPTION NA     kept     K6   
#>  4          4 ACPI_NUMA        ACPI_NUMA        NA      OPTION NA     kept     K6   
#>  5          5 IA64_GENERIC     IA64_GENERIC     NA      OPTION NA     kept     K6   
#>  6          6 NUMA             NUMA             NA      OPTION NA     kept     K6   
#>  7          7 IA64_DIG         IA64_DIG         NA      OPTION NA     kept     K6   
#>  8          8 IA64_HP_ZX1      IA64_HP_ZX1      NA      OPTION NA     kept     K6   
#>  9          9 X86              X86              NA      OPTION NA     kept     K6   
#> 10         10 X86_PC           X86_PC           NA      OPTION NA     kept     K6   
#> 11         11 IA64_SGI_SN2     IA64_SGI_SN2     NA      OPTION NA     kept     K6

When something is wrong

A dead feature

Let us break the model on purpose. The example miband3_dead.uvl is a copy of the Mi Band 3 with one more constraint: NFC => !ContactlessPayment (“a band with NFC has no contactless payment”). But constraint 3 says that contactless payment needs NFC.

dead <- vp_generate(vp_example("miband3_dead.uvl"))
dead
#> variplex model "miband3_dead"
#>   features: 10 variable (the nodes of the graphs), 8 core, 1 dead
#>   requires: 20 arrows   excludes: 10 lines
#>   at least one: not computed (use vp_generate(or_graph = TRUE))
#>   atomic sets: 1 (of two or more features)
vp_features(dead) |> filter(status == "dead")
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>   feature            status
#>   <chr>              <chr> 
#> 1 ContactlessPayment dead

No error: the model is still valid. But ContactlessPayment is now dead. It can never be selected, because selecting it would need NFC and forbid NFC at once. A dead feature is a feature that exists on paper only; the list of dead features is the first thing to look at after changing a model.

The broken model: ContactlessPayment, in red, is dead. Green features are core; yellow ones are the abstract features, which variplex leaves out.

A model without any product

Now a worse mistake: a constraint that demands BT40 & Screen, while constraint 5 forbids it.

void <- tryCatch(
  vp_generate(vp_example("miband3_void.uvl")),
  error = function(e) e
)
class(void)
#> [1] "variplex_void_model" "variplex_error"      "error"               "condition"
conditionMessage(void)
#> [1] "the formula 'miband3_void.dimacs' is unsatisfiable (void model): no configuration exists, so no graphs were written. Look for contradictory constraints in the model; the summary miband3_void__summary.json records \"void\": true.\n  The model has no valid configuration: every feature is dead."

The model is void: no configuration satisfies all the constraints, so the product line has no product. There are no configurations, so there is nothing to say about pairs of features, and no graphs are written; only the summary is, with "void": true.

Errors and their classes

Every error of vp_generate() has the class variplex_error and a more precise one, so that a program can react to each kind; the field exit_code is the exit code that the command line of Strong4VM gives for the same problem:

Class exit_code Meaning
variplex_usage 1 An argument has a value that is not accepted.
variplex_input 2 The input is wrong: it is not a valid model or formula.
variplex_void_model 3 The model is void: it has no valid configuration.
variplex_solver 4 The solver failed.
variplex_unknown_name 5 A name was not recognised (only with unknown_names = "error").
variplex_strict_uvl 6 A constraint could not be translated (only with strict_uvl = TRUE).
variplex_check_failed 7 A consistency check failed.

A value that an argument does not accept is answered with what was expected:

vp_generate(vp_example("miband3_realized.uvl"), tristate = "sometimes")
#> Error in `match.arg()`:
#> ! 'arg' should be one of "merge", "builtin", "both"
